newsitem.title: USA: Dow hits new high amid merger fever, bonds slacken.
newsitem.headline: Dow hits new high amid merger fever, bonds slacken.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks surged to another record high Tuesday amid a spate of mergers and as the dollar remained strong despite falling from its highest level in nearly three years against the German mark.
Bonds weakened as its three-week rally showed signs of running out of steam.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 78.50 points at 7,067.46 after closing above the 7,000 level for the first time ever Thursday.
It was the 13th record close so far this year for the 30-stock blue-chip index as big-name companies extended their run as the favoured class on Wall Street.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,509 to 1,036 on moderate volume of 474 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Standard & Poor's 500 stock index and NYSE Composite index also ended in record territory.
Analysts said a number of factors played into the rally, including the flurry of merger deals, and, somewhat ironically, a heightened sense of caution about the market.
"People are cautious," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co. "People are buying quality. People are buying more liquid names."
Keeping with a recent trend, the session was fairly uneventful until the final moments, when a wave of computer programme buying propelled the Dow sharply higher.
Analysts said the dollar's recent strength also figured in the stock market's rally.

"With the dollar acting as well as it has, foreign investors have stepped up their buying," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "They tend to focus on the large-cap stocks because they're more liquid."

Currency traders called time out in the dollar's rally, as the U.S. currency fell from its highest level in nearly three years against the mark and the German currency benefited from a slump in both the Italian lira and British pound.

Mounting fears that Italy will not be a member of the first group of European nations forming a single currency and fading expectations for a Bank of England interest rate rise caused the currencies of those nations to drop.
After reaching a new high of 1.7050 marks, the dollar fell to 1.6850 marks in late trading from 1.7015 at Monday's European close. The U.S. market was closed Monday for the Presidents Day holiday.
The dollar fell to 123.90 yen from 124.35 in late European trade on Monday. The dollar hit a high of 124.71 yen during Tuesday's trading, a bit below its recent high of 124.82 yen.
The 30-year Treasury bond fell 8/32, or $2.50 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.55 percent from 6.53 percent Friday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Coffee prices tumbled as a week-old strike ended in Colombia and sparked a wave of profit-taking by speculators.

Coffee for May delivery fell 9.75 cents to 157.25 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar, and Cocoa Exchange in New York. The May contract hit a high of 172.25 cents Friday, capping a 70 percent climb during a two-month run-up.
Corn prices rose sharply, boosted by heavy buying by investment funds.
March corn rose 8-3/4 cents to $2.82-3/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade after hitting $2.83, its highest level in almost four months.
Overseas, London's leading FTSE 100 index of shares ended 5.5 points lower at 4,332.3. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average fell 279.90 points, or 1.49 percent, to close at 18,470.75.
